There were significant differences in patient’s actual and desired level of knowledge. 2 Some patients reported wanting to “live in a bubble” (FG1.3) and did not wish to 3 know anything beyond the essential information; such as when their appointments 4 were. On the other hand, other patients kept detailed records of their blood scores 5 (e.g. free-kappa-lambda ratio). For these patients, feeling informed created a sense 6 of empowerment through feeling that they were an active participant of their care. 7 These patients were able to describe the link between MGUS and MM and lymphoma 8 and define the progression risk to MM “1% per annum“ (TI.4). Other patients 9 reported their knowledge as low to medium and many desired to improve their 10 knowledge. 11

12

Patients who did not receive information leaflets at diagnosis reported more 13 extensive online knowledge seeking than those who did. Patients described their 14 experiences of searching for MGUS information online as challenging and websites 15 difficult to navigate; with most of the information using unfamiliar and complex 16 language or referring to information in other countries (especially the USA). As a 17 result, many patients were linked/directed to MM (not MGUS) information, which 18 caused significant anxiety and worry particularly if identified shortly after diagnosis. 19 Patients illustrated how they found negative and fear-inducing stories when 20 searching online at diagnosis; as they lacked the understanding to differentiate 21 MGUS and MM information. 22

“I sort of looked up what MGUS was .I looked up online and I sort of had a fair idea 23

what it was well sort of an idea what it was so I was probably a wee bit apprehensive 24

because I thought it’s possible-…I could not have cancer but I could possibly be 25

getting cancer so I did feel a bit (shocked) “. TI.2 26

Patients interacted with HCPs in order to gain information in relation to MGUS to 28 educate and empower themselves. Patients sought information from three types of 29 HCP; their haematology team (doctors and clinical nurse specialists), their GP and 30 personal contacts within healthcare who were HCPs. 31

32

Patients described how receiving good communication from their haematology team 33 at diagnosis facilitated less anxiety and greater understanding. Good communication 34 was described as the HCP taking the time to explain the condition and providing 35 written materials at diagnosis. 36

Most patients described being diagnosed incidentally when being investigated for 4 non-related medical issues, such as high blood pressure, co-morbidity appointments 5 (e.g. asthma), hospitalisation for acute illness (e.g. pneumonia) and acute injuries 6 (e.g. knee trauma). Typically, elevated paraprotein was initially investigated in the 7 haematology department, which interviewees said was located within the “cancer 8 centre”, which generated fear and anxiety for some patients. 9

In one case, a patient previously under investigation for MM was relieved to have 10 been diagnosed with MGUS; as they were not a “cancer patient” (FG1.1). Therefore, 11 their experience of entering the MGUS health services was more positive than many 12 of the other participants. 13

“I have to say this, because this (location of haematology) really 14

irked me, and I think it was because it was done over in (Local 15

Hospital’s Cancer Centre). That very place. God bless everyone”. 16

FG1.3 17

18

All patients were under surveillance via a telephone clinic and are informed of the 19 results of their surveillance-mandated blood tests by the haematology clinical nurse 20 specialists. This typically includes a discussion of the blood result scores, inquiries 21 about the patient’s general health and an opportunity for patient questions. Some 22 patients kept a record of their blood results at each appointment. Patients were 23 overwhelmingly satisfied with telephone surveillance, with none discussing negative 24 experiences. 25

The telephone clinic offered an alternative to hospital-based consultant-led 26 appointments by offering collaborative management between the haematology 27 clinic and their primary care physician. The telephone clinic was reported to be more 28 convenient and was especially beneficial for rural patients, for whom visiting the 29 hospital and consultant in another town/city was seen as burdensome and time- 30 consuming. Patients also reported that telephone follow-up helped to reduce anxiety 31 as they were able to avoid seeing cancer patients at the cancer centre (a reminder of 32 what their diagnosis could progress to). Patients perceived the telephone clinic 33 reduced burden on secondary care services (haematology staff especially 34 doctors/consultants) and were supportive of improvements made to the service. 35

“I think that -- that telephone follow up is --is a Godsend.“ FG1.6 36

“The telephone clinic I think to me that’s probably really all I need it would seem, it 1

would seem to me you know an awful waste of time to come down and taking up 2

the doctor’s time in the hospital or anything I mean this is only a… quick telephone 3

“Well, whenever I have the telephone appointment with the nurse I feel there’s a 5 little bit-… I’m wondering what I’m going to be told am I getting worse or is my 6 health deteriorating. So I’d be glad whenever the conversation’s finished.” FG2.1 7

8

Despite an overall sense of satisfaction, most patients worried about the telephone 9 clinic but realised that it was necessary. The waiting period between testing and 10 results, which can be weeks, was highlighted as challenging. Patients reported 11 anxiety during this waiting period and wondered if the blood tests would reveal an 12 increase in disease markers and/or reveal progression to cancer (MM). 13

14

Patients encountered a range of communication styles from healthcare professionals 15 when being diagnosed and when they sought MGUS information. The style of 16 communication mediated their experience of the health service and overall 17 satisfaction. Some patients reported excellent psychosocial care, with clinicians 18 (specialists and primary care physicians) taking time to explain the MGUS diagnosis, 19 which led to less diagnosis-related anxiety with patients reporting that they felt 20 informed and supported. Haematology nursing staff were seen as having a positive 21 communication style. Nurses provided reassurance, reduced anxiety and provided 22 “peace of mind” through their psychosocial care, provision and explanation of 23 information. Participants reported feeling more comfortable speaking with nurse 24 specialists than doctors. 25

26

Other patients reported fewer positive interactions with doctors and recalled how 27 these negative experiences were linked to feelings of isolation and uncertainty about 28 their diagnosis, especially immediately post-diagnosis. Some patient’s reported 29 doctors in haematology not taking the time to describe their condition and being 30 detached and dismissive of MGUS patients. While patients understood that other 31 patients (especially cancer patients) required more care, they were disappointed at 32 the lack of psychosocial care and empathy; with no/limited signposting to other 33 information or being able to talk to someone about their diagnosis. This resulted in 34 some patients having increased anxiety and feeling less informed. 35

“Classic consultant. They go in and out of that every day, and they don't see it. They 36

see people a lot worse that you. And they’re just delivering a line, to say, "Away you 37

Patients discussed a sense of isolation/uncertainty regarding their diagnosis, which 4 many patients felt could be alleviated by providing support structures for meeting 5 and interacting with other MGUS patients. MGUS patients are often not supported by 6 cancer support charities or groups and can feel in “limbo” (FG1.1), both in cancer 7 services and supportive structures such as the voluntary sector. Patients proposed 8 developing two structures; in-person support groups (similar to cancer support 9 groups) and volunteer peer support (local) contactable MGUS patients’ post- 10 diagnosis, for questions or concerns. Travel and low patient numbers were identified 11 as threats to the long-term stability of in-person meet-ups. Focus group attendees 12 (compared to telephone interviewees) were more positive about meetings/support 13 groups. Some patients valued the availability of a contactable MGUS patient who 14 they could speak to over a “coffee or glass of wine” FG2.1. Developing this indirect 15 support may be useful addressing this unmet need. 16

17

“There's nothing (to help coping if individuals are struggling). you 18

know, I just get through it, eventually. But it's not like I can lift the 19

phone and ring (FG1.3). Lift the phone and ring (FG1.4), and say 20

"How are you feeling today?" You know, "I'm feeling pretty (poor)". 21

There's nothing out there, there's nobody out there. And that's 22

because we're in limbo.” FG1.1 23

24

Discussion 25

This novel study highlights the potentially negative impact that receiving and living 26 with a MGUS diagnosis can have on patients, particularly at the point of diagnosis 27 and time of follow-up appointments. Although receiving an MGUS diagnosis rarely 28 had a life-changing impact, it did cause patients to re-evaluate their lives and to 29 question their mortality. Most patients had a poor level of understanding of MGUS. 30 Patients highlighted some issues in current MGUS service provision, especially in 31 relation to information provision, but were positive about active surveillance 32 provided by the nurse-led telephone clinic. Information was a powerful tool for 33 patients, with good information and communication giving rise to improved 34 understanding and reduced anxiety. The lack of available support for patients and 35 their unwillingness to talk about MGUS to their families and friends, due to their own 36 poor knowledge about MGUS and to avoid causing others anxiety was an issue for 37 some patients. 38

1

The emotional impact of MGUS was complex and nuanced to each individual. At the 2 initial diagnosis, all patients reported experiencing shock at being diagnosed with an 3 asymptomatic condition linked to cancer. This shock was similar to that reported for 4 receiving positive results from population-level cancer screening (De Morgan et al., 5 2002; Prinjha et al., 2011), other premalignant conditions (Gough et al., 2003; 6 Hounsgaard et al., 2007; Kennedy et al., 2008; Shylasree et al., 2008) and 7 haematological malignancies (Swash et al., 2016). For many patients, this shock 8 developed into anxiety and fear; the potential of developing cancer remained an 9 active concern in the weeks and months following diagnosis. This is similar to the 10 experiences of MM patients who reported having a sudden and shocking 11 confrontation with their mortality, by a condition that they had never heard of 12 (Hauksdóttir et al., 2017). This anxiety often regresses when chronic illness patients 13 become accustomed to their diagnosis and the uncertainty is reduced (Mishel, 1999); 14 similar to the experiences reported by the MGUS patients in this study. MGUS 15 patients outlined the initial diagnosis period as having the highest psychosocial 16 impact on their lives and an area where intervention could be implemented in the 17 future. As most of the patients were several years’ post-diagnosis, further research on 18 newly diagnosed patients may provide greater insight into immediate impact of 19 receiving a MGUS diagnosis. 20

21

Knowledge of MGUS was one of the strongest messages from the collective voice of 22 the participants. Overall, patients had poor knowledge of MGUS at diagnosis. There 23 was a clear distinction between the patients with MGUS knowledge and those with 24 less knowledge. Those with more knowledge appeared to experience less anxiety 25 and improved coping. In the wider MM literature, MM patients reported the initial 26 gathering of information and developing knowledge as important to acquaint 27 themselves with their condition and reduce their distress (Hauksdóttir et al., 2017). 28

29

Patients are often unable to absorb verbal information at diagnosis (Kessels, 2003). 30 Anxiety and isolation can result if the information from HCPs is considered to be 31 lacking, confusing, or inadequately explained (Prinjha et al., 2011). Many MGUS 32 patients reported not receiving an information leaflet at diagnosis, one of the most 33 frequent sources of healthcare information for patients (Kenny et al., 1998; Meredith 34 et al., 1995). However, there may be a recall bias in not recounting receiving the 35 information. However in our previous research, only 42% of haematologists provided 36 information booklets at all diagnoses (McShane et al., 2017). Nevertheless, receiving 37 an information leaflet was linked to a more positive post-diagnosis experience. While 38 acknowledging their condition may be lower priority for their doctor’s time 39

(compared to cancer patients), the need for more doctor-patient communication and 1 psychosocial care for MGUS patients was highlighted. Online searching was 2 described as difficult with patients reporting contradictory and confusing 3 information about MGUS. This finding is not surprising as haematological 4 malignancies have previously been reported as being among the least well 5 understood malignancies by patients (Department of Health, 2012). 6

7

The telephone clinic was universally preferred to the hospital clinic by patients for 8 reducing anxiety related to visiting the “cancer place”, and convenience (time and 9 travel reasons). The telephone clinics, where the participants were recruited, follow 10 the outreach model as proposed by Rawstron et al. (2007). Our study adds to the 11 growing literature of positive patient-reported experiences with telephone clinics 12 (Rawstron et al., 2007) and suggests that CNS-led clinics are a useful addition to 13 MGUS service provision. The COVID-19 pandemic has increased tele- 14 medicine/remote monitoring, which may accelerate development of MGUS 15 telephone clinics nationally and internationally. Some patients felt their wait time 16 between phlebotomy and receiving results was too long and extended their anxiety. 17 It would therefore be useful for service providers, to consider mechanisms to reduce 18 the length of this waiting period. 19

20 MGUS patients were often reluctant to share details of their diagnosis with others 21 outside their immediate family circle, due to low awareness and the feeling that 22 other’s issues were more important; especially if cancer related. This was felt by some 23 participants as obstructing their ability to cope with the diagnosis. Compared to the 24 support available for cancer patients, MGUS patients felt peer support and support 25 groups were lacking. Similar to other premalignant conditions (De Morgan et al., 26 2002; Dowswell et al., 2012; Kennedy et al., 2008), MGUS patients agreed that there 27 was benefit in meeting other patients to discuss shared experiences. Patients 28 attending the focus groups reported positive experiences in being able to see and 29 talk (often for the first time) to others with MGUS. An official website featuring life 30 stories and blogs was also advocated by patients. This style is in keeping with 31 mainstream health websites including ‘NHS Choices’ in the United Kingdom and 32 charity websites who aim to supplement scientific facts with experiential information 33 (Kelly et al., 2013). 34 35 Clinical Implications 36 37 A number of clear considerations came from the patients in this study. 38 39

1. In line with the UK/Nordic guidelines (Bird et al., 2009), patient-friendly 1 information and support is necessary at the point of diagnosis and thereafter for 2 MGUS patients. Information booklets are available (e.g. Myeloma UK, Macmillan 3 and the International Myeloma Foundation), however our results suggest these 4 are not routinely provided at diagnosis. The information should be offered in 5 various formats (verbal, paper and online) as patient needs differ. Information 6 should advise on future follow-up procedures, disease progression and 7 signs/symptoms to be aware of. Inclusion of ‘life stories’ of other MGUS patients 8 in information leaflets was also suggested by patients who want to ‘see’ what 9 other MGUS patients look like. 10

11

2. Many patients were diagnosed/followed-up initially in the local hematology 12 department, however patients recalled this negatively as the ‘cancer place’ 13 owing to cancer patients receiving their treatments in the same department. 14 Improving the clinical environment may reduce patient anxiety, improve 15 knowledge absorption and reduce future psychosocial distress. 16 17 3. The use of telephone clinics was positively endorsed by MGUS patients in this 18 study. Telephone clinics reduce patient burden by reducing hospital visits, which 19 can incur both financial and psychosocial costs (Overend et al., 2008; Rawstron et 20 al., 2007);the feasibility of expanding this service should be explored 21 22 Strengths and limitations 23 Our study is based on the lived experiences of 14 MGUS patients in two health and 24 social care trusts in Northern Ireland. Our sample size is comparable to other 25 premalignant studies which have reported on small sample sizes (under 16) 26 (Hounsgaard et al., 2007; Kennedy et al., 2008; Lee Mortensen and Adeler, 2010; Likes 27 et al., 2008; Prinjha et al., 2006; Pruitt et al., 2008). Despite a small sample data, 28 However, despite this, we feel as a research team that this was an accurate 29 representation of the views of NI MGUS patients but that there were further insights 30 that could found with more participants in some sub-themes, which may have not 31 reached data saturation. 32

When considering the transferability of our findings to the wider MGUS population, 33 the younger age of participants (present study 55.9 vs 74 years old; Li et al., 2016), 34 and low risk MGUS profile should be considered. Due to the small numbers and 35 similar age range (predominantly 50-70 years old), we were unable to explore the 36 impact of age on experiences However, as patients diagnosed with MGUS at a 37 younger age live longer with the knowledge of their condition and have an increased 38 lifetime risk of developing MM; this younger group may receive a greater benefit 39 from future interventions. 40

Combining the focus group and interview data has potential drawbacks. The 1 increased interaction and sharing in the focus group led the data into different 2 avenues which were not as dynamic in the dyadic interviews. These diversions 3 provided greater insight of the lesser acknowledged and thought-of aspects of an 4 MGUS diagnosis. Correspondingly, the in-depth nature of interviews and individual 5 experiences provided finer details. Combining these modalities can cause 6 disconnects between the experiences of focus group and interview participants and 7 required the analysis to consider if the modality influenced this. However, we found 8 the codes and themes were consistent during the analysis of both modalities. The 9 use of the patient’s CNSs as recruiters opens the possibility of recruitment bias, 10 however this is a common recruitment mechanism in premalignant conditions 11 (Kennedy et al., 2012; Pruitt et al., 2008). Information was not collected on those who 12 did not indicate interest in participating 13

14

Conclusions 15 Life-long surveillance provides patients with a periodical reminder of their MGUS 16 diagnosis and its potential progression to cancer, which can cause anxiety. Measures 17 such as provision of information leaflets to all patients at diagnosis, patient support 18 groups, improved HCP communication and diagnosis/follow-up within a non-cancer 19 clinical environment may help improve health and psychosocial wellbeing of MGUS 20 patients. 21 22 23 Conflicts of Interest and sources of Funding Statement 24 The authors have declared no conflict of interest exists. The corresponding author 25 had full access to all the data and final responsibility for the decision to submit for 26 publication. Funding for this study was provided by a Cancer Translational Research 27 Group Young Investigator Grant. At the time of the study, Dr Charlene McShane was 28 in receipt of a Cancer Research UK Population Sciences Research Fellowship. 29 30

Purpose: 1 The aim of this study was to investigate patient experiences of living with 2 monoclonal gammopathy of undermined significance (MGUS). Living with a 3 premalignant condition such as MGUS may elicit negative psychosocial effects 4 including increased anxiety and fear of progression to cancer. To date, no study 5 utilising qualitative methodology has explored the lived experiences of MGUS 6 patients. 7

Methods: 8 Data was collected via two focus groups and six telephone interviews. MGUS patients 9 (n=14) were recruited via nurse-led hematology telephone-clinics in Northern 10 Ireland. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and the data subjected to thematic 11 analysis. 12 13 Outcome: 14 Thematic analysis identified 3 overarching themes; (1) The psychosocial impact of an 15 MGUS diagnosis, (2) Knowledge of MGUS and (3) Experiences of MGUS health 16 services. Patients with MGUS reported experiencing poor psychological adjustment 17 to their condition particularly at the point of diagnosis and approaching follow-up 18 appointments. Feelings of isolation, poor information-provision, increased 19 uncertainty and limited psychosocial support for MGUS patients were also reported. 20 Patients did however reflect positively on their experience of being followed up via 21 nurse-led telephone clinics. 22 23 Conclusions: 24 Provision of patient friendly information guides at diagnosis, and additional 25 psychosocial support services such as nurse-led telephone clinics and coordinated 26 patient groups may help MGUS patients adjust better to their diagnosis and in doing 27 so improve quality of life in this patient population. 28 29 30 Key words: 31 Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), multiple myeloma, 32 Quality of life, Qualitative, Precancer. 33 34

Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is an asymptomatic 1 premalignant blood disorder which precedes multiple myeloma (MM), an incurable 2 B-cell malignancy (Kyle et al., 2006). The annual rate of progression to MM and 3 related lymphoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia, 4 and lymphoma has been reported to be 1% (Kyle et al., 2002), meaning the vast 5 majority of individuals diagnosed with MGUS will not progress to MM. MGUS is more 6 common in males (Wadhera and Rajkumar, 2010), and individuals of black ethnicity 7 (Landgren et al., 2007, 2006). Younger age at diagnosis has been reported among 8 black individuals (median age of diagnosis: 66 vs 70 years old (white individuals ) 9 (Landgren et al., 2017). MGUS prevalence is estimated to be 3.2% in adults over 50 10 years old, however, most individuals remain undiagnosed due to the asymptomatic 11 nature of presentation (Kyle et al., 2006; Therneau et al., 2012). 12

13

MGUS patients often experience considerable hospital activity pre- and post- 14 diagnosis, implying diagnosed cases are living with comorbidities (Lamb et al., 2019). 15 MGUS is typically detected incidentally during investigations for other conditions, 16 with an elevated total protein level leads to serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) 17 which detects a paraprotein (International Myeloma Working Group, 2003; Kyle et al., 18 2010). Individuals are diagnosed when a reduction of one or more immunoglobulin 19 class (IgG, IgA and IgM) levels are detected from a serum protein electrophoresis 20 (SERP) test (Bird et al., 2009). The International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) 21 defines the parameters of MGUS as having a serum M protein <30g/l, <10% clonal 22 plasma cells (PCs) in the bone marrow and, most importantly, the absence of end- 23 organ damage that can be attributed to the PC proliferative disorder or other B-cell 24 proliferative disorders (International Myeloma Working Group, 2003; Kyle et al., 25 2010). Once diagnosed, it is recommended that MGUS patients are followed-up 26 regularly (every 3-12 months) to identify early signs of progression to MM (Bird et al., 27 2009; Smith et al., 2007). Within the UK, this is often conducted by clinical nurse 28 specialists (CNS) utilising telephone clinics for low-risk patients; under the guidance 29 of haematology consultants (Rawstron et al., 2007). 30

31

Studies investigating the quality of life of patients with haematological precancerous 32 conditions is limited. Design 6 This study was a qualitative design, which utilised an integration of focus groups and 7 telephone interviews to collect and integrate the data. The Consolidated Criteria for 8 Reporting Qualitative Studies (COREQ) (Tong, Sainsbury, & Craig, 2007) guided the 9 reporting of the study. Participants were identified using convenience sampling and 10 recruited during their routine telephone surveillance appointment by CNS’ at two 11 Healthcare trusts (Belfast and Southern) in Northern Ireland. During these 12 appointments the CNS discusses patient’s blood test results and assesses their 13 general health; with a goal of identifying potential signs of progression such as 14 increased infections, bone pain and/or fractures (Rawstron et al., 2007). All patients 15 on telephone follow-up were considered low risk for progression. 16 17 Prior to invitation, the CNS assessed each patient against eligibility criteria. 18 Individuals were not eligible if they were considered to be too frail or had 19 neurocognitive difficulties or severe mental health issues which could affect their 20 ability to provide consent. The CNS introduced the study to participants during their 21 routine telephone appointment. Interested patients were mailed a study information 22 pack (containing a study information booklet, a consent sheet, a contact information 23 sheet, a pen and a prepaid envelope to return the consent and contact information 24 forms) by the CNS. Suitable times for the focus group/interview were then organised 25 by the university-based study team by telephone call. Non-responders received a 26 reminder telephone call from the CNS after two weeks. No patient had a prior 27 relationship with the research team; the latter was separate to the clinical team 28 involved in recruitment. Prior to recruitment, study documentation was reviewed by 29 a subset of (non-MGUS) patients in the Northern Ireland Clinical Trials Centre 30 ‘Personal and Public Involvement in Research’ committee. 31

The psychosocial impact of an MGUS diagnosis 1 The first major theme identified was the psychosocial challenges of an MGUS 2 diagnosis and how this fluctuated across the MGUS pathway. In particular, patients 3 discussed heightened emotions at diagnosis, including shock and fear. Interaction 4 with cancer services also invoked social comparisons with cancer patients and 5 increased fears of progression. 6

7

Patients described their diagnosis as “the shock of my life” (TI.2), with some viewing 8 their diagnosis as an existential threat to their future. Patients reported completing 9 wills and purchasing cemetery plots. These patients wanted more information and 10 appeared to have been more anxious at diagnosis than other participants. However, 11 all patients were aware of the potential for progression to cancer and reported some 12 initial anxiety relating to this. 13

“To realise that this had the potential to be cancerous was a shock and it certainly 14

made me think about my mortality which I had-…obviously had thought about 15

before but I thought about it even more and I did make a will and I did buy a grave 16

(laughing). Basically I thought “Right I better start getting organized, just in case this 17

leads to something awfully terrible”. TI.2 18

For many patients, the shock developed into anxiety post-diagnosis; with patients 19 describing consistent thoughts about their mortality during this time. The impact of 20 the diagnosis and hearing the term ‘cancer’ led to some missing important MGUS 21 information during the initial consultation. This shock and anxiety was present until 22 their follow-up appointment, usually 3 months’ post-diagnosis; when patients could 23 ask questions and process the information better. 24

25

The psychosocial impact seemed to reduce over time; as patients came to terms with 26 their condition. Most patients had lived with MGUS for many years and their worries 27 about the consequences lessened over time. Their fear of progression to cancer was 28 compared to “Damocles sword” FG2.2; a consistent but mainly dormant fear. Their 29 fear that their next appointment could be the appointment they received bad news 30 from the CNS and had progressed to cancer. 31

“I think it's sort of a Damocles, hanging very high-- you know, it sort of-- not likely-- 32

Sort of a high percentage chance of not developing anything”. FG2.2 33

34

For some patients, MGUS was a spur to improve their lives and make lifestyle 35 changes, with patients reporting increased physical activity and improving their diet 36 to lessen their risk of progression. 37

MGUS was often overshadowed by medical issues of friends/family, especially if 7 cancer-related. Patients felt that their MGUS diagnosis was less important and tried 8 to avoid causing worry and anxiety by not talking about their MGUS diagnosis. As a 9 result, some patients felt isolated with their diagnosis; having no-one to speak to 10 about their worries. Male participants were particularly reluctant to speak about their 11 MGUS diagnosis due to their lack of understanding about the condition and burden 12 this may place on their families/friends. The asymptomatic nature led to some 13 patients comparing it to a mental health diagnosis; where patients were healthy on 14 the outside but unwell inside. 15

“Cause it's asymptomatic, so there are no symptoms associated with MGUS. It's 16

seems to be that it's a hidden illness. So that may be one of the reasons why people 17

don't really know much about it.” FG2.2 18

Patient’s knowledge of MGUS 20 The second major theme identified was how patient’s knowledge of MGUS affected 21 the MGUS experience; particularly around acquiring knowledge from HCPs and the 22 Internet. While some patient-friendly information helped patients to be more 23 confident about their diagnosis and take an active role in their own care, poor 24 information led to decreased psychosocial wellbeing. 25

26

Patients found the full name (monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined 27 significance) difficult to understand, remember and explain to others; such as family 28 and friends. Confusion was heightened by the differing terminology used by HCPs 29 when they were trying to explain the condition to patients. Patients reported that 30 MGUS was described to them by HCPs as a; “protein deficiency” (FG1.4), “raised 31 protein” (TI.4)”, “benign blood abnormality” (TI.2) and a “rogue blood in my system” 32 (TI.3). Many felt this was a contributing factor to their confusion and anxiety at 33 diagnosis. 34
